t: Introduction: low temperature and forensic medical examination
n: In this lecture we will consider the effect of low temperature on the body and its forensic medical examination. The general effect of high and low temperature leads to heat stroke or general hypothermia, and the local effect to a burn or frostbite. The body is more resistant to low than to high temperature. In almost all cases the effect of low temperature on the body occurs as a result of an accident. Attention, there is a risk of error: general hypothermia relates to the whole body, while frostbite relates to a part of the body. In frostbite the general body temperature is normal.

t: Body temperature and heat loss
n: About body temperature and heat loss. In normal conditions body temperature is 36–37 °C. Heat is lost by radiation 55 %, sweat 27 %, conduction 15 % and various secretions 3 %. At a temperature below 22–25 °C or above 43–44 °C, changes incompatible with life occur. A rise or fall in body temperature from the norm disturbs the activity of the body.

t: Factors predisposing to low temperature
n: We group the factors predisposing to low temperature. External factors: low temperature, high humidity and wind; they intensify the effect of low temperature. Internal factors: fatigue, hunger, illness, hypodynamia, and also clothing unsuited to the season and alcohol intoxication. Sensitive age groups: children and the elderly are considerably more sensitive to the effect of low temperature. Remember: in almost all cases the effect of cold occurs as a result of an accident.

t: General hypothermia and frostbite: the difference
n: Let us clearly distinguish general hypothermia from frostbite. The general effect of low temperature leads to general hypothermia, and the local effect to frostbite. In general hypothermia the whole organism is affected, body temperature falls, and stages of compensation and decompensation are seen. In frostbite, however, a part of the body is damaged: the extremities, ear, nose, cheek. The general temperature is normal, and only one area is chilled. There is a latent and a reactive period, and 4 degrees are distinguished. On a corpse after death from general hypothermia, signs of local frostbite are usually absent.

t: General hypothermia: concept and conditions
n: The concept and conditions of general hypothermia. The effect of low temperature over a certain time disturbs the mechanisms of thermoregulation and lowers body temperature. High humidity, strong wind, clothing unsuited to the season, immobility, fatigue and intoxication predispose. A negative temperature is characteristic of general hypothermia, but it may develop even on prolonged stay in air up to +10 °C. Death usually occurs after several hours of exposure in air, and in cold water in about 1–1.5 hours.

t: Children and newborns
n: About children and newborns. Young children, especially newborns, are very sensitive to low temperature. The elderly are also quite sensitive. The first reason: the mechanisms of thermoregulation are not fully formed. The second reason: the relative surface area of the body in relation to mass is large, so heat is lost quickly. In rapid death, S. M. Vishnevsky's spots, that is small haemorrhages in the stomach, are infrequent, so in children they are often not found.

t: The role of alcohol intoxication
n: The role of alcohol intoxication. Alcohol dilates the skin vessels. For this reason heat loss from the body is intensified still more. An intoxicated person cannot assess the situation correctly and does not take measures of protection against chilling. Alcohol in large amounts disturbs the activity of the thermoregulation centres, that is the heat-control centres. Attention: in severe intoxication the body may not be in the posture of a person frozen to death. The absence of a posture does not exclude the effect of cold.

t: Time of death in cold water and in air
n: The time of death in cold water and in air differs. In cold air death from general hypothermia usually occurs after several hours, sometimes more. In cold water this time is much shorter, 1–1.5 hours, and the reason is the rapid development of chilling. On sudden immersion in cold water, death may occur before deep hypothermia, from vascular collapse, that is collapse, or cold shock.

t: First stage: compensation
n: The first stage is called compensation. At first the body switches on compensatory mechanisms and tries to keep body temperature normal. So that more heat is produced, the function of all systems of the body is intensified. Metabolism increases, liver and muscle glycogen decreases, and oxygen consumption in tissues rises. At the same time the skin vessels constrict and heat loss decreases. When the compensatory capacities are exhausted, decompensation begins and body temperature begins to fall.

t: Second stage: decompensation
n: The second stage is decompensation. When compensation has ended, body temperature begins to fall; first of all the activity of the CNS, that is the central nervous system, is disturbed. At +30…+28 °C the function of the cerebral cortex is disturbed, breathing and pulse slow down, and pressure falls. As a result hypoxia develops and metabolism decreases. If temperature falls by 1 °C, biochemical processes in tissues slow down by about half.

t: Final stage and cause of death
n: The final stage and cause of death. In the final stage body temperature falls to +25…+22 °C. Death often occurs from primary cessation of breathing. In some cases the cause is vascular collapse or ventricular fibrillation of the heart. Let us briefly repeat the stages. The first is compensation: temperature strives toward normal, metabolism increases, the skin vessels constrict. The second is decompensation: the CNS is disturbed, breathing and pulse slow. The third is the final stage: respiratory arrest, collapse, fibrillation.

t: Simpson: classification of hypothermia and temperature limits
n: Classification of hypothermia and temperature limits after Simpson. Hypothermia is the fall of body temperature from 37 °C to below 35 °C; an environment below 10 °C is enough for harmful hypothermia in a frail person. Classification: mild hypothermia 32–35 °C, moderate 30–32 °C, severe below 30 °C; below 32 °C shivering stops. Loss of consciousness may occur at 27–30 °C; ventricular fibrillation and apnoea below 27 °C. Cold water takes heat 20–30 times faster than dry air, and alcohol, by dilating vessels, increases heat loss.

t: Simpson: signs by degree of hypothermia
n: Signs by degree of hypothermia after Simpson. In the mild degree: shivering, sensation of cold, apathy, cold pale skin. In the moderate degree: uncontrolled violent shivering, confusion, impaired coordination, loss of memory, drowsiness, disturbance of speech, slow shallow breathing and weak pulse. In the severe degree: loss of control of the limbs, shivering that stops suddenly, loss of consciousness, absence of breathing and pulse, muscle stiffening, dilated pupils. For hypothermia the weather need not be unusually cold: even in a moderately cold winter many elderly people become hypothermic.

t: Quick question: stages and temperature
n: Quick questions, stages and temperature. Question: which system is disturbed first in decompensation? Answer: the CNS, that is the central nervous system, then the function of the cerebral cortex. Question: how do the vessels and pulse change at +30…+28 °C? Answer: peripheral vessels dilate, pulse slows, pressure falls. Question: what is the cause of death at +25…+22 °C? Answer: most often primary cessation of breathing; collapse or fibrillation are also possible. Attention, risk of error: although there is enough oxygen in the blood, hypoxia develops in the tissues; they are not the same thing.

t: Case analysis 1: an intoxicated person found in the cold
n: The first case analysis: an intoxicated person found in the cold. Situation: in a cold, damp and windy open place a person in a state of intoxication was found. The clothing is unsuited to the season. Question: which factors predisposed to general hypothermia? External factors: low temperature, high humidity, wind. Internal factors: clothing unsuited to the season, fatigue, hunger, illness, immobility, alcohol intoxication. Alcohol, by dilating skin vessels, intensifies heat loss. An intoxicated person cannot assess the situation correctly and does not protect himself. Attention: do not think that general hypothermia occurs only at a negative temperature. With prolonged stay it may develop even at an air temperature up to +10 °C.

t: Examination of the corpse: the "posture of a person frozen to death"
n: In examining the corpse, the posture of a person frozen to death is important. At the place of death the corpse is in this posture, and it testifies to the vital effect of low temperature. The arms are drawn to the chest, the legs bent to the abdomen. In this way the victim tries to retain body warmth. In this position the heat-radiating surface of the body is considerably reduced. Attention: in those in severe intoxication this posture may be absent. The absence of the posture does not at once exclude general hypothermia.

t: Skin signs: Raysky's sign and "goose skin"
n: Skin signs: Raysky's sign and goose skin. Under prolonged vital effect of low temperature, the exposed parts of the body are cyanotic and slightly swollen. Around the mouth and nostrils ice icicles are found, and hoar frost on the eyebrows and eyelashes. These are called M. I. Raysky's signs. In some cases the muscles that raise the hair contract and the skin takes on the appearance of goose skin. Sometimes in men the testis is shrunken and the scrotum drawn up to the inguinal canal. This is K. V. Puparev's sign.

t: Puparev's sign and melting of snow
n: Puparev's sign and melting of snow. Sometimes in men the testis is shrunken and the scrotum drawn upward to the inguinal canal. This is K. V. Puparev's sign. In some cases the muscles raising the hairs contract and the skin takes on the appearance of goose skin. If the victim lay on snow, the snow melts from the warmth of the body. Then, under the action of cold, a layer of ice appears under the body. Attention: the layer of ice is not a specific sign of low temperature. It forms also when a corpse that has not yet cooled is laid on snow.

t: Colour of cadaveric lividity: positive and negative temperature
n: The colour of cadaveric lividity differs at positive and negative temperature. Because there is much oxygen in the blood, the skin and cadaveric lividity have a pinkish-red hue. At positive temperature, up to +10 °C, tissues manage to use up oxygen even after brain death, so the colour of the lividity is bluish-violet. At negative temperature much oxygen remains in the blood, a bluish-violet hue is not seen, and the lividity is pinkish-red.

t: Cooling, rigor of the corpse and signs of frostbite
n: Cooling, rigor of the corpse and signs of frostbite. In an environment of low temperature the corpse cools faster. Rigor mortis begins later and is weak. On a corpse after death from general hypothermia of the body, signs of local frostbite are usually not seen. Exception: if during life an attempt was made to warm up, mainly degree I, sometimes degree II frostbite is found on the corpse. Attention: distinguish general hypothermia from local frostbite. They are separate types of injury.

t: Case analysis 2: conclusion from external signs
n: The second case analysis: conclusion from external signs. Situation: in winter a corpse was found in an open place. The arms are drawn to the chest, the legs bent to the abdomen, and there is hoar frost on the eyebrows and eyelashes. The exposed skin is cyanotic, slightly swollen; around the mouth and nose, ice icicles. The cadaveric lividity is pinkish-red. Question: what do these signs indicate? The posture, hoar frost and ice icicles indicate the vital effect of low temperature. Attention: a layer of ice under the snow is non-specific, and appears also in a corpse that has not yet cooled. In severe intoxication the posture may be absent.

t: Internal examination: general signs
n: Internal examination and general signs. The internal organs are congested, and all tissues are of a pinkish-red hue. Because of the slow death, bright red blood with clots is found in the left chamber of the heart and the aorta, and also in the large arteries. The stomach is empty and considerably reduced in size; this is Pukhnarevich's sign. Remember: the slow tempo of death is the reason for the finding of blood with clots.

t: Fabrikantov's sign and the urinary bladder
n: Fabrikantov's sign and the urinary bladder. Because of increased permeability of vessel walls, diapedetic haemorrhages are found in the internal organs. Small haemorrhages in the mucosa of the renal pelves are called Fabrikantov's sign. Because of disturbed innervation and paralysis of smooth muscle, the urinary bladder is full of urine. Attention: Fabrikantov's sign is in the renal pelvis, whereas Vishnevsky's spots are in the stomach, sometimes in the mucosa of the duodenum. Do not confuse these two signs.

t: Vishnevsky's spots: the main sign
n: Vishnevsky's spots are regarded as the main sign. Small haemorrhages are found in the mucosa of the stomach, sometimes the duodenum. These spots occur in 80–90% of deaths from general hypothermia and have important diagnostic significance. The diameter is ≤0.5 cm, and they lie on the crest of a fold. They may be detected even 6–9 months after death.

t: Vishnevsky's spots: mechanism of formation
n: The mechanism of formation of Vishnevsky's spots. Low temperature disturbs the autonomic nervous system, in particular the trophic function of the solar plexus. Vasomotor changes raise the permeability of the vessel wall, and diapedesis of erythrocytes occurs. In the area of haemorrhage, necrosis of the mucosa occurs; this is a haemorrhagic infarct caused by spasm. Then, under the action of hydrochloric acid, acid haematin forms.

t: Vishnevsky's spots: time and age factor
n: Vishnevsky's spots and the factor of time and age. If death from low temperature occurs rapidly, Vishnevsky's spots are very few or may be absent altogether. For this reason in young children this sign is often not seen. If death comes after several hours or more, numerous haemorrhages are found in the mucosa. With time the haemorrhages intensify, and in their place erosion, then ulcer appears; perforation and bleeding may be complications.

t: Simpson: corpse findings and behaviour in hypothermia
n: Corpse findings and behaviour in hypothermia after Simpson. A pinkish-violet patch over large joints, that is elbow, hip, knee, cold erythema, is found in about 50 per cent of deaths from hypothermia. Under the microscope there is no extravasation of erythrocytes, which distinguishes it from a bruise. Haemorrhagic erosions in the stomach, that is Vishnevsky's spots, are non-specific: they occur also in sepsis, shock and alcohol abuse. Paradoxical undressing and the hide-and-die syndrome can make the scene look suspicious; the latter is seen more often in slow chilling.

t: Quick question: internal signs
n: Quick question on internal signs. Question: a change in which organ is named after which scientist? Match the signs of Pukhnarevich, Fabrikantov and Vishnevsky. Pukhnarevich's sign: the stomach is empty and considerably reduced. Fabrikantov's sign: small haemorrhages in the mucosa of the renal pelves. Vishnevsky's spots are in the gastric mucosa. Kasyanov's sign relates to the straight tubules of the kidneys. Attention, risk of error: Fabrikantov's sign is in the kidney, Vishnevsky's spots in the stomach.

t: Microscopic and histochemical examination
n: Microscopic and histochemical examination. Under the microscope, spasm, swelling, small haemorrhages and bronchospasm are found in the microcirculation. A change in the epithelium of the straight tubules of the kidneys is called M. I. Kasyanov's sign; proliferation and necrobiosis are seen in the tubules. In histochemistry, glycogen and adrenal lipoids disappear. In brief death, in ice-cold water and wind, blood sugar may fall while liver glycogen is preserved.

t: Laboratory assessment of alcohol
n: Laboratory assessment of alcohol. In severe intoxication, if cold acts, alcohol in the blood may be low and in the urine high. This is explained by strong utilisation of alcohol by the body in cold conditions. Alcohol dilates the skin vessels and heat loss is intensified; in intoxication danger is wrongly assessed. In heavily intoxicated people the posture of a person frozen to death may be absent.

t: Freezing of the corpse: distinguishing it from vital injuries
n: Freezing of the corpse and distinguishing it from vital injuries. A corpse, regardless of the cause of death, may freeze at sub-zero temperature; various injuries then appear. Attention: injury resulting from freezing is not a vital injury, and they must be distinguished. On freezing, the brain and parenchymatous organs increase in volume; in the skull this may lead to fracture of bones. In the cranial cavity the brain expands as it freezes, the bone breaks, and the sutures separate. Under the microscope numerous small cracks and separation of the epidermis from the dermis are seen. In the chest and abdomen volume increases, but there is no serious change.

t: Thawing a frozen corpse and its effect
n: Thawing a frozen corpse and its effect. Frozen corpses are usually thawed at room temperature, then examined forensically. Thawing may take several days; the time is shortened by warm air or hot water, up to +50 °C. Rapid thawing intensifies haemolysis of erythrocytes, that is blood haemolysis, and post-mortem imbibition of tissues. As a result imbibition of blood and tissue arises.

t: Case analysis 3: a frozen corpse found
n: The third case analysis: a frozen corpse found. Situation: a corpse frozen at sub-zero temperature was brought in; cracks in the skull bones and separation of the sutures were found. A frozen brain, increasing in volume, can break the skull bones, separate the sutures and rupture the soft tissues from within. Question: is this a vital injury or a result of freezing? Which signs and which examination help? The way is as follows: check whether the neck froze before the head, and whether small cracks and separation of the epidermis are present under the microscope.

t: Local effect of low temperature: frostbite
n: The local effect of low temperature is called frostbite. With an entirely normal body temperature, frostbite develops when temperature falls in a separate area. It is most often an accident; the extremities, ear, nose and cheek are affected. Often the 1st toe at the heel and the 3rd–4th finger on the palm freeze. Spasm, then paralysis, of vessels slows or stops circulation, and tissue nutrition is disturbed. The periods are as follows: in the latent period the area is chilled, then the area begins to warm, this is the reactive period, and by depth degrees I–IV are established.

t: Degrees of frostbite (I–IV)
n: The degrees of frostbite, I to IV. In the reactive period four degrees of frostbite are distinguished by depth of injury. In degree I there is a reddish-bluish hue, oedema and itching, lasting 3–7 days. In degree II blisters with clear fluid appear, 10–20 days, without a scar. In degree III there is necrosis of skin and a haemorrhagic blister, 1–2 months, and a scar remains. In degree IV there is necrosis to the bone, the area is shed, and a scar remains. After degrees I and II, heightened sensitivity to cold persists in the affected area for a long time. In degree IV purulent infection, that is phlegmon, lymphangitis, phlebitis, osteomyelitis and sepsis, is often added.

t: Repercussion, complications and severity criteria
n: Repercussion, complications and severity criteria. Repercussion: when one arm or leg is frostbitten, changes may also appear in the opposite limb. In the medical document it is important to note the circumstances of the case, the fall in temperature of the area, and the degree and area. Criteria for life-threatening frostbite are given in relation to body surface: degree II > 20 %, degree III > 15 %, degree III–IV > 10 %. In our region frostbite as an object of examination is encountered very rarely.

t: Case analysis 4: a victim with frostbite
n: The fourth case analysis: a victim with frostbite. Situation: a person who stayed long in cold, damp air has blisters with clear fluid on the fingers of the hands, and the surrounding skin is cyanotic and slightly swollen. This picture corresponds to degree II frostbite: blisters appear on days 1–2 and pass in 10–20 days without a scar. Question: what should be recorded in the document? The circumstances of the case, the fall in local temperature, the degree of frostbite and the area of the affected region. Attention: recording only the degree is not enough; the area is also stated. Degree II frostbite of more than 20% of the surface is life-threatening.

t: Diagnosing general hypothermia: the set of signs
n: Diagnosing general hypothermia and the set of signs. Forensic medical diagnosis relies on the specific signs of death from general hypothermia. External signs: posture and hoar frost on the eyebrows and eyelashes are vital signs, but in an intoxicated person they may be absent. A layer of ice under snow is non-specific and also forms on a corpse that has not cooled. Internal sign: Vishnevsky's spots in the stomach occur in 80–90% of cases; in rapid death they are few or absent. Microscopic sign: change in the straight tubules of the kidneys, that is Kasyanov's sign. Remember: ice under the snow is a non-specific sign, whereas Vishnevsky's spots are an important sign.

t: Conclusion
n: Conclusion. Sensitivity to low temperature is increased by humidity, wind, clothing unsuited to the season, fatigue, hunger and alcohol. Children and the elderly are more sensitive. First there is compensation, then decompensation. When temperature falls to +25…+22 °C, death most often occurs from primary cessation of breathing. On a frozen corpse, fracture of the skull bones and separation of the sutures are possible. Such changes must be distinguished from vital injuries. In frostbite the degree and area are stated: more than 10% of degree III–IV, more than 15% of degree III or more than 20% of degree II are life-threatening.
